Causal disruption of piriform cortex beta-band oscillations will impair perceptual constancy by increasing the trial-by-trial correlation between physical odor concentration and perceived intensity, indicating that top-down beta feedback normally suppresses concentration-dependent variability in subjective odor intensity.

Experimentally enhancing beta-band feedback from the piriform cortex to the olfactory bulb via frequency-specific transcranial alternating current stimulation at the individual beta peak will increase perceptual constancy by reducing trial-to-trial variability in perceived intensity for identical physical concentrations, whereas disrupting beta-phase alignment will abolish this effect.

Top-down beta-band feedback from the piriform cortex to the olfactory bulb implements a predictive coding mechanism for odor intensity, such that biasing participants' prior expectations about upcoming intensity while holding physical concentration constant will shift olfactory bulb gamma-band encoding and piriform cortex–olfactory bulb phase-amplitude coupling toward the expected intensity rather than the actual stimulus concentration.

When odor intensity is predicted by a prior cue, top-down beta-band feedback from the piriform cortex to the olfactory bulb and the strength of OB-PC beta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling will scale with the discrepancy between predicted and actual intensity, such that larger prediction errors produce stronger late beta-gamma interactions even at identical physical concentrations.

Providing valid trial-by-trial cues about upcoming odor intensity will reduce PC-to-OB beta–gamma phase–amplitude coupling and PC beta burst rates when the delivered odor matches the expected intensity, whereas invalid cues will enhance coupling and shift perceived intensity ratings toward the cued expectation, indicating that top-down beta feedback conveys an intensity prediction rather than merely reflecting post-hoc perceived intensity.
